newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia kills off pioneering euthanasia law.
newsitem.headline: Australia kills off pioneering euthanasia law.

text.p: The Australian parliament overturned the world's first and only euthanasia law on Monday, nine months after the Northern Territory introduced it to let terminally ill people commit assisted suicide.

The upper house of parliament, the Senate, voted 38 to 33 in favour of a backbencher's bill, already passed by the lower house, that broke constitutional convention by intervening in the territory's affairs to quash its euthanasia law.
Leading euthanasia campaigner doctor Phillip Nitschke, who has helped four people die under the law, immediately burned a copy of the bill outside the Senate in protest at the vote.
He said the Senate had dashed the hopes of two terminally ill people in the territory who had completed legal formalities and were preparing to kill themselves.
"The Senate of Australia betrayed the terminally ill in Australia," Nitschke told reporters.
"They've betrayed, especially, the two people who are dying in the Territory tonight."
The vote followed an unusually heated debate in which one euthanasia supporter challenged his opponents to explain themselves to people who sought suicide as a release from pain.

"How can you say: 'We will not let you do it, we intervene, we know better than you do, notwithstanding your pain, your suffering, your indignity'?" Greens senator Bob Brown asked anti-euthanasia senators.

Four people have legally killed themselves, using a machine that injects a lethal drug through a computer programme, since the outback Territory's legislation came into effect in July. The first was 66-year-old cancer patient Bob Dent, who used it in September to end what he called "a roller-coaster of pain".
Euthanasia has remained illegal in the rest of Australia, but supporters and opponents agree that it is widely practised informally.

Senators did not vote according to party lines on Monday but the anti-euthanasia bill had the support of conservative Prime Minister John Howard, who told parliament in December: "I think there have got to be some absolutes in life, and respect for human life is one of those.
"I know that's not a popular view of a lot of people if you read the polls, but that's my personal view."
Anti-euthanasia campaigners said Howard was out of touch with public opinion. Polls show that about 75 percent of Australians back voluntary euthanasia.
In quashing the law, Canberra has also taken the extraordinary step of overriding the laws of the Northern Territory, whose people elect their own legislature.

The federal parliament could not have intervened had one of the six more autonomous states passed the euthanasia law and euthanasia campaigners have promised to continue their battle in state parliaments.
The anti-euthanasia bill was first proposed by a Christian backbencher in Howard's ruling coalition, Kevin Andrews.
Andrews argued that legalising voluntary euthanasia might open the floodgates to lawful killing.
Some even argued that there was only a small step between voluntary and involuntary euthanasia, and the next development might be the killing of people who could not consent.

The Senate rejected a last-ditch attempt to limit the anti-euthanasia bill to a life of two years and also a move to exempt the two dying people who had already obtained the necessary doctors' signatures to use the territory law.
Nitschke said those two people might now seek a doctor who would break the law to help them die.
"They can go back and try to find someone who will help them illegally," he said.
They could also write to Governor-General William Deane, who must go through the formality of signing the bill into law.
Pro-euthanasia supporters said Deane could delay the bill long enough for doctors to legally help the two die.
